job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Bianca Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live in a shared student house in São Paulo with four other women, and my day starts with a list on my phone. Mornings are classes for my master's in accounting, afternoons are the library or applying for jobs, and on weekends I answer phones at a physiotherapy clinic for a small wage. I try to cook on Sundays for the whole week, because it saves money.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Can you tell me how you got here?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did a business administration bachelor's and passed with an average mark, no internship, because every firm wanted people already in their third year of an accounting degree. My father drives a city bus and my mother sells cosmetics door to door, so nobody can pay my fees. I took a private loan of about 90,000 reais. I'm doing the accounting master's so that I can sit the professional exam and be taken seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds fine to me. I'd keep it practical: use the tools that work, ignore the ones that don't. I'd say it to my housemates, and to my father who thinks robots are about to take his bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's the same pressure as now. There are a few accounting offices near me and lots of graduates, so I'd still be knocking on doors. Repayment starts after the course, around 1,100 reais a month, which is nearly my whole clinic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, sit the professional exam in March, and apply to small accounting offices, not just big firms, about 12 a week. I'd keep the clinic weekends. I'd also keep using the AI chat now and then to translate papers and tidy my cover letters, since classmates do and it helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A low hum of worry, like a fridge that never switches off. I'm not frightened, just always counting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the loan repayments if you don't get a job by the end of the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a grace period from the lender and take a second weekend job, maybe tutoring bookkeeping to first-years. My housemates would lend me food, if not money. I'd be thin, but not on the street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who helps you with job leads, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My professor Dona Marta sends me small-office openings, which is how I know most firms are family-run and hire people they trust. I've started going to the professional association's evening talks to be seen.

say: I'd say it's fine and we should **use what works** and ignore the rest.
I'd tell my father robots aren't about to take his bus.
think: The pressure is the **same as now**: few offices near me and many graduates.
Repayment of about 1,100 reais a month would eat my whole clinic wage.
do: Apply to **12 small accounting offices** a week.
Keep the clinic weekends and ask the lender for a grace period.
feel: A **low hum** of worry, like a fridge that never switches off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the normal pattern, a new tool and a reshuffle, and the firms that are smart will keep some people to check the machines. I'd also say everyone should learn to use the tools a bit, even if reluctantly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the entry-level seats shrink. Entering invoices, matching bank statements and preparing the monthly tax forms are the first jobs I'd be given, and they're the first things software can do. A firm that needs five juniors will need two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the tools properly, not just now and then. I'd practise on the accounting software that small offices use, because Dona Marta says her contacts pay for people who can run it. I'd also keep the exam plan, since a certified person has something a machine can't have: a signature that the law accepts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not desperate. I can see where I might stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which accounting tasks would move to software first, in your view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Invoice entry, bank matching, standard tax forms. What stays is the signature and the talking to the owner who doesn't understand why the tax is so high.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide whether to keep going in accounting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the exam still matters, if offices still hire certified people for those parts, I'd stay. If a year after I qualify there are no junior jobs left, I'd go into something like payroll consulting or admin for clinics, where I already know the people.

say: I'd say it's the **normal pattern**: new tools, a reshuffle, and smart firms keep people to check.
I'd say everyone should learn the tools a bit.
think: Entry-level seats **shrink**: a firm needing five juniors will need two.
The first tasks I'd be given are exactly what software does.
do: Practise on the **accounting software** small offices use.
Keep the exam plan, because a certified **signature** is something the law accepts.

feel: **Anxious but not desperate**, since I can see where I might stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should keep calm and ask the government and the big firms to say what they'll do. I'd say it carefully, because panic doesn't help, but I'd be pushing for answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be in trouble. Accounting is thinking work, and a firm that can have it done cheaply by software won't take on a graduate with an average mark and no internship. The loan of 90,000 would still be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the exam preparation if I couldn't afford it and look for any hands-on job, like at the clinic, where the physiotherapists need people who can touch and move patients. I'd ask the clinic for full-time hours. I'd also sit down with my parents and see what we could cut, though they have little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel my chest tighten when I think of the loan letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father would say a bus driver also sees the end coming, and we'd both laugh a little. Then we'd do sums on the kitchen table. I'd say I'd come home to save rent if I had to, even though I like my independence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you expect to step in during those two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect the government to give money for a while. A country can't have millions of graduates with debt and no jobs, but I'd still act as if no one's coming.

think: Firms won't hire a graduate with an **average mark** and no internship.
The **90,000** loan would still be there.

fieldNote: Practical to the end: she keeps asking who will **step in** and plans without them.

steps.text: Ask the physiotherapy clinic for full-time hours
Pause the exam course if the fees can't be paid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to adapt, but it isn't a lot. I'd say people should keep their options open and pick a skill that involves another person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be nervous but not lost. I'd have time to finish the master's, qualify, get a first job, and shrink the loan. By 2031 I'd be 29, and I'd want to be somewhere that machines make my work better, not replace it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first job in a small firm, even badly paid, and learn the software they use. I'd send 400 reais a month to the loan, and keep 100 for a rainy day. I'd also stay on at the clinic if they let me, since it's a place where I'm known.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but workable. It feels like a long hike with a hill at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently if you saw it coming for five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The exam. A recognised qualification is the one thing that travels with me from job to job. If the firm closes, I'm still certified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you not give up, even under pressure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd prepare for the exam, take the first job, and use any spare hour to practise the tools. I'd talk to Dona Marta every few months so I hear about openings before they're posted.

I'd tell people to pick a skill involving another person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good amount of time, though people should still prepare instead of hoping. I'd say get a skill that machines can't copy easily, like trust with clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be mostly fine. I'd have my qualification, a few years at a firm, and the loan gone or nearly. What I'd worry about is my parents' generation, who can't retrain easily, and who I'll probably be helping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, take a first job in an office, and aim for a role with client contact, such as tax advice for small businesses. I'd keep learning the tools every year. And I'd start saving for my parents, maybe 200 a month, because I'll probably need to help them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite calm. A practical sort of calm, with a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger self about taking this loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a risk, but understandable. Without the loan I couldn't have studied at all, so I'd not regret it, only wish I'd got an internship in the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the next ten years look like if all goes reasonably well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A first job by 2028, a better one by 2032, loan done by 2035. And some savings for my mum and dad. That's the plan, and I'd keep a list of it on my phone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2-year one worries me most, because the loan and my average mark go together badly with no time. What would help is a pause on repayments, a real chance at a first job, and honest information from the government.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd cook. I'd cook for my housemates every Sunday whatever happens, because a full table makes it easier to talk about scary things.

headlineQuote: A full table makes it easier to talk about scary things.
portrait: Bianca is a **24-year-old** accounting master's student in São Paulo with a 90,000-reais loan, an average mark and no internship.
She is **centre** and practical: asks who will step in, then plans as if no one will.
She is **steady** with AI, using it for translation and letters, and shifts to regular use once it pays.
Her mood stays **anxious** in most worlds and alarmed in the 2028 one, always tied to the loan.
Her **father drives a bus** and her mother sells cosmetics, so the family cannot pay her fees.
biggestWorry: Bianca fears **2028** most, because the loan and her average mark collide with no time.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a **pause on repayments**, a real shot at a first job and honest information.
